title: ARIA buttons, links and menu items need names
summary: An element with role button, link or menuitem has no accessible name. Add visible text or an aria-label so people know what it does.
problem: An element with role="button", role="link" or role="menuitem" has no accessible name. It usually holds only an icon, so assistive technology can announce its role but not its purpose.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear that a control exists but not what it does, so they must guess or skip it. Voice control users cannot say the name of a control that has none.
steps: Find the element in the scan result. It is a non-native control with a command role.
Give it a name. Visible text inside it is best. For an icon-only control, add aria-label with a short action, such as "Close".
Hide the decorative icon itself from assistive technology with aria-hidden="true" so it does not add noise.
Better still, replace the element with a native <button> or <a href>, which also adds keyboard support.
whyItMatters: A control with no name cannot be used with confidence, and icon-only close and menu buttons are often the way out of a task. This is a WCAG Level A requirement, the level that accessibility regulations and procurement requirements commonly build on.
howToCheck: Select the element in your browser's accessibility inspector and confirm its Name is not empty. A screen reader should announce the name along with the role.
